## Overview

Almost everything else in pecotmr needs LD. Fine-mapping from summary
statistics needs it, RSS weight learning needs it, colocalization needs it,
and the heritability estimators are built on nothing else. The pipelines
handle it for you, so this vignette is about the layer underneath: the two
kinds of LD reference pecotmr reads LD from, computing LD from genotypes,
checking it is usable, and reducing a variant set that is too correlated to
model.

```{r load-packages}
library(pecotmr)
```

## Two kinds of LD reference

Every pipeline reads LD from one place: the LD reference of the collection
row it is working on. A collection can use one reference for every row or a
different one per row; `ldReference()` lists the distinct references, each
stored once. A reference is one of two things (or a mixture of either,
below).

- A **genotype panel**, read lazily from disk with `readGenotypes()`. LD is
    computed on demand for whichever variants a step needs, so a panel far
    larger than any one region costs nothing until it is read. It is the same
    structure a `QtlDataset` holds its genotypes in.
- An **`LdMatrix`**: a correlation matrix you built, held in memory. pecotmr
    does not read pre-computed LD from disk; read the matrix with whatever
    suits its format and wrap it.

### A genotype panel

```{r panel}
panel <- readGenotypes(
    plink2Prefix = file.path(
        system.file("extdata", "ld_reference", "chr22", package = "pecotmr"),
        "protocol_example.LD.chr22"
    )
)
panel
```

The bundled panel is a *stochastic LD sketch*: 1,000 pseudo-samples
projected from 60 real people, which reproduces their LD without carrying
their genotypes. pecotmr recognises one by its `.afreq` sidecar and records
the real sample size and allele frequencies on the panel when it is read,
because the projected dosages say nothing about either:

```{r panel-sketch}
S4Vectors::metadata(panel)$ldProjection
head(SummarizedExperiment::rowRanges(panel)$AF)
```

A MAC cutoff or DENTIST's truncation rank counts the 60 real samples, and
ldsc's unbiased \(r^2\) and HDL use the effective size of the sketch's LD,
\(1 / (1/60 + 1/1000) \approx 57\). Neither is the 1,000 columns.

`computeLd()` correlates any subset of a panel's variants:

```{r panel-ld}
R <- computeLd(panel)
dim(R)
```

A panel can also be reached through an LD meta file: one row per chromosome
or block, giving its coordinates and the genotype files behind it, with
paths relative to the meta file. `readGenotypes(ldMeta = , block = )` opens
the whole block whose row covers the window.

### An LdMatrix

```{r ldmatrix}
ld <- LdMatrix(R, nSamples = 57)
ld
```

The matrix's dimnames here are `chrom:pos:A2:A1` ids, so the variants are
parsed from them; otherwise pass `variants`, a `GRanges` or a data frame with
`chrom`, `pos`, `A1` and `A2` (and optionally `SNP` and `AF`). Correlations
must be signed by the dosage of `A1`. `nSamples` is the number of samples the
LD was estimated from, and `AF`, the frequency of `A1`, is what the
frequency filters and cTWAS's weight scaling read.

`LdMatrix()` checks the matrix's shape and labels, its unit diagonal, that
its entries lie in \([-1, 1]\), and its symmetry. It does not check positive
semi-definiteness, which costs an eigendecomposition; `checkLd()` below does.

A matrix has no genotypes, so the steps that need them work differently:

| Step | With an `LdMatrix` |
|---|---|
| LD for any variant set | read from the matrix |
| MAF / MAC filters, cTWAS scaling | need `AF` (and `nSamples` for MAC) |
| DENTIST, ldsc's unbiased \(r^2\), HDL | need its `nSamples` |
| Missingness filter | refused: there are no genotypes to be missing |
| RAiSS | inverts the matrix instead of the genotype SVD |

### Mixtures of LD references

Summary statistics meta-analysed across ancestries are correlated through
the weighted average of the cohorts' LD. `LdMatrix()` builds that average
from one `LdMatrix` per cohort, matching the components by position and
allele and keeping the variants they all cover:

```{r mixture}
half <- seq_len(ncol(panel) / 2)
ldA <- LdMatrix(computeLd(panel[, half]), nSamples = 30)
ldB <- LdMatrix(computeLd(panel[, -half]), nSamples = 30)
LdMatrix(list(ldA, ldB), mixtureWeights = c(0.7, 0.3))
```

The weights are typically each cohort's share of the GWAS sample size.

`GenotypeMixture()` builds the same average from genotype panels, but
lazily: the panels stay on disk and are read only for the variants a step
asks about, so each keeps answering for its own samples. A frequency or
missingness filter judges every panel on its own and drops a variant that
fails in any of them. The mixture is a `MultiAssayExperiment` with one
experiment per cohort, so the panels are named after their cohorts, and
`experiments()` and `sampleMap()` show what it holds.

```{r genotype-mixture}
GenotypeMixture(
    list(EUR = panel[, half], AFR = panel[, -half]),
    mixtureWeights = c(EUR = 0.7, AFR = 0.3)
)
```

### Using a reference

Either kind is passed the same way, and from there every step reads it the
same way. One reference serves every row; a list gives each row (each study,
for `GwasSumStats`) its own:

```{r use, eval=FALSE}
gwas <- GwasSumStats(..., ldReference = panel) # or ldReference = ld
gwas <- GwasSumStats(..., ldReference = list(panelA, panelB)) # per study
```

When two collections meet in one pipeline — a QTL and a GWAS side in
colocalization, say — each QTL row and the GWAS rows it is combined with must
use the same reference: two panels must share their samples and allele
coding, two `LdMatrix` objects must agree on the LD they share, and a panel
never matches a matrix. `colocboostPipeline()` is the exception: it reads each
side's LD from that side's own reference, so the two may differ.

## Computing LD from genotypes

`computeLd()` takes a dosage matrix and returns the correlation matrix:

```{r compute}
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(100 * 20), 100, 20, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("v", 1:20)))
X[, 5] <- X[, 4] + rnorm(100, sd = 0.01) # a near-duplicate pair
R2 <- computeLd(X)
dim(R2)
```

`method` selects the estimator — `"sample"` (default), `"population"`, or
`"gcta"` — and `shrinkage` applies shrinkage toward the identity. `backend`
can hand the work to SNPRelate or snpStats when those are installed.

## Checking that LD is usable

A correlation matrix estimated from finite samples is usually not positive
definite, and methods that invert it or take its eigendecomposition will
fail or return nonsense. `checkLd()` reports the diagnosis. Run it on the
real panel rather than the toy matrix above, which is well conditioned by
construction:

```{r check}
diagnosis <- checkLd(R)
diagnosis[c(
    "isPd",
    "isPsd",
    "minEigenvalue",
    "nNegative",
    "conditionNumber"
)]
```

That is what a real reference looks like: positive *semi*-definite but not
positive definite, with a smallest eigenvalue at rounding scale (`-7e-16`)
and a condition number around `1e9`. The negative value is floating-point
noise on a rank-deficient matrix, not structure — but it is exactly what
makes an unguarded `sqrt()` or `solve()` fail, and why LDER clamps
eigenvalues before forming its weights.

`method = "shrink"` or `"eigenfix"` returns a repaired matrix instead of a
report:

```{r check-fix}
fixed <- checkLd(R, method = "eigenfix")
c(before = diagnosis$minEigenvalue, after = checkLd(fixed$R)$minEigenvalue)
```

The smallest eigenvalue is lifted off zero, though on a matrix this
rank-deficient it stays tiny — repair makes the decomposition safe, it does
not restore rank that the reference panel never had. Repairing also changes
the data, so prefer a better-conditioned variant set where you can, which is
what the next section is for.

## Reducing a correlated variant set

Two variants in near-perfect LD carry the same information, and a design
containing both is singular. Three tools address that, differing in what
they optimise.

`ldPruneByCorrelation()` drops variants until no pair exceeds a correlation
threshold, keeping the choice arbitrary among equivalents:

```{r prune}
pruned <- ldPruneByCorrelation(X, corThres = 0.8)
ncol(pruned$X.new)
pruned$filter.id
```

It returns the reduced matrix and the retained column indices, so a parallel
table of statistics can be subset the same way.

`ldClumpByScore()` keeps the *best-scoring* variant in each LD clump rather
than an arbitrary one — pass PIPs or −log10 p-values as `score` and it
behaves like PLINK's clumping:

```{r clump, eval=FALSE}
ldClumpByScore(X, score = pips, chr = chrom, pos = position, r2 = 0.2)
```

`enforceDesignFullRank()` is the targeted version: rather than thresholding
everything, it drops variants iteratively until the design plus its
covariates reaches full column rank, and stops there.

```{r full-rank}
Xdup <- cbind(X, dup = X[, 1]) # exactly collinear
dim(enforceDesignFullRank(Xdup, C = matrix(1, nrow(Xdup), 1)))
```

The `C` argument is the covariate matrix the design will sit alongside —
rank has to be assessed on the combined matrix, since a variant can be
independent of the other variants yet collinear with a covariate.
`strategy` chooses what to sacrifice: the most correlated variant, the
lowest-variance one, or the one least correlated with the response.

## Aligning summary statistics to a panel

The counterpart to all of this is on the summary-statistics side: variants
must exist in the panel, and their alleles must be oriented the same way.
`filterVariantsByLdReference()` and `mergeVariantInfo()` do that, and are
covered in the [QC vignette](rss-qc.html), where the motivation lives.
